```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4)
```

This follows Part A of *Week 7 — Exercise 2* (27200 Data-driven Bioengineering), translated from
Python to R and applied to the heart valve disease data set (Nordmeyer et al. 2023, PRIDE PXD023800).

**Design.** The 75 left-ventricle biopsies come from three groups (aortic stenosis, mitral
regurgitation, donor-heart controls), each with women and men. Patients of the **same sex and the same
disease group** are treated as **biological replicates**. This report compares one disease group with
the controls of the same sex. Sections A1–A8 walk through one comparison step by step; section A9
then runs the same pipeline for **all comparisons** (aortic stenosis vs control, mitral regurgitation
vs control, aortic stenosis vs mitral regurgitation), separately for women and men.
To change the step-by-step comparison, change the `params` at the top
(e.g. `sex: "male"` or `case: "mitral regurgitation"`), or knit from the console:

```r
rmarkdown::render("PartA_heart_valve_proteomics.Rmd",
                  params = list(sex = "male", case = "mitral regurgitation"))
```

**What differs from the benchmark.** In the notebook the true answer was known (human proteins
unchanged, E. coli up 3-fold). Here it is not, so the "check against the truth" step (A8) becomes
"what did we find, and how much does it depend on our choices?".

Only base R and `readxl` are used, so the code reads like the Python version step by step.

```{r load}
library(readxl)

samples <- read_excel(params$file, sheet = "samples")
pg      <- read_excel(params$file, sheet = "proteinGroups", guess_max = 20000)  # one row per protein group
dim(pg)

# Replicate groups = disease group x sex
table(samples$group, samples$sex)
```

```{r groups}
# The samples (LFQ columns) of the two groups we compare
ctrl_cols <- samples$column[samples$group == params$control & samples$sex == params$sex]
case_cols <- samples$column[samples$group == params$case    & samples$sex == params$sex]
lfq       <- c(ctrl_cols, case_cols)
short     <- sub("LFQ intensity ", "", lfq)                 # e.g. "AS_03_F"
is_case   <- lfq %in% case_cols
grp_col   <- ifelse(is_case, "#D62728", "#1F77B4")         # red = disease, blue = control

cat(sprintf("control: %d %s samples   |   case: %d %s samples\n",
            length(ctrl_cols), params$sex, length(case_cols), params$sex))
```

The table is MaxQuant output with the columns you need:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Protein IDs`, `Majority protein IDs` | proteins that share the peptides of this row (a *protein group*) |
| `Gene names` | gene name(s) of the group |
| `Reverse` | `+` if the group is a decoy |
| `Potential contaminant` | `+` for common contaminants (keratin, trypsin, serum proteins, …) |
| `Only identified by site` | `+` if seen only through a modified peptide |
| `LFQ intensity <sample>` | label-free quantification value per sample; 0 means not measured |

# A1 · Filter

```{r filter}
is_plus <- function(x) !is.na(x) & x == "+"

keep <- !is_plus(pg$Reverse) & !is_plus(pg$`Potential contaminant`) &
        !is_plus(pg$`Only identified by site`)

cat(sprintf("removed: %d decoys, %d contaminants, %d only-by-site\n",
            sum(is_plus(pg$Reverse)), sum(is_plus(pg$`Potential contaminant`)),
            sum(is_plus(pg$`Only identified by site`))))

d <- pg[keep, ]
cat(sprintf("kept %d protein groups\n", nrow(d)))
```

# A2 · Log-transform

Intensities span several orders of magnitude and are skewed. On the log scale they are roughly normal,
and a **fold change becomes a difference** (a doubling is +1, a halving −1 in log2).

```{r log}
raw <- as.matrix(d[, lfq])
raw[raw == 0] <- NA                    # 0 means "not measured", not "zero protein"
X <- log2(raw)
colnames(X) <- lfq

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(raw[, 1], breaks = 60, main = "raw intensity", xlab = "intensity", col = "grey70", border = "white")
hist(X[, 1],   breaks = 60, main = "log2 intensity", xlab = "log2 intensity", col = "grey70", border = "white")
```

# A3 · Missing values

Not every protein is measured in every sample. Look at *which* ones are missing.

```{r missing, fig.height = 4.5}
cat("missing values per sample:\n")
print(colSums(is.na(X)))

# Split proteins into ten groups by average intensity, and ask how often each group is missing
mean_int     <- rowMeans(X, na.rm = TRUE)
frac_missing <- rowMeans(is.na(X))
ok  <- is.finite(mean_int)                                   # proteins seen in at least one sample
dec <- cut(mean_int[ok], quantile(mean_int[ok], 0:10 / 10), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = 1:10)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
barplot(tapply(frac_missing[ok], dec, mean), col = "#1F77B4",
        xlab = "average log2 intensity (deciles, low to high)", ylab = "fraction missing",
        main = "Missing values are mostly low-abundance proteins")
```

Missing values are concentrated among the weakest proteins: most are missing because the protein was
**below the detection limit**, not at random.

A protein measured in only a few patients cannot be tested fairly. In the notebook (3 replicates)
the rule was *at least 2 of 3 values in both conditions*; with larger groups we use the same
proportion: **at least two thirds of the samples in both groups**.

```{r valid}
n_min_ctrl <- ceiling(round(params$min_valid * length(ctrl_cols), 6))
n_min_case <- ceiling(round(params$min_valid * length(case_cols), 6))

valid <- rowSums(!is.na(X[, ctrl_cols])) >= n_min_ctrl &
         rowSums(!is.na(X[, case_cols])) >= n_min_case
X <- X[valid, ]
d <- d[valid, ]

cat(sprintf("required: >= %d of %d controls and >= %d of %d cases\n",
            n_min_ctrl, length(ctrl_cols), n_min_case, length(case_cols)))
cat(sprintf("%d proteins left, %d missing values remain (%.1f%%)\n",
            nrow(X), sum(is.na(X)), 100 * mean(is.na(X))))
```

# A4 · Normalize — and check the assumption

Samples never contain exactly the same amount of material, so intensities differ between runs for
technical reasons. **Median normalization** shifts every sample so that its median is the same.

It assumes that **most proteins do not change between the conditions**. In the benchmark this was
false (a large share of the proteins were E. coli, all going up). In heart tissue it is a reasonable
assumption: disease changes some proteins, not most of them. If it holds, the median log2 fold change
over all proteins should be close to 0.

**Does this still make sense with biological replicates?** Yes. Normalization corrects for
*technical* differences between MS runs (how much material was loaded and how sensitive the instrument
was that day), and every patient sample is a separate run. Whether the replicates are biological or
technical makes no difference to that. Normalization only removes a **global shift of a whole
sample**. The variation between patients in individual proteins stays in the data, and that variation
is what the t-test needs. What matters is whether the assumption holds: if disease changes the
*composition* of the tissue, a shift in the median can be real biology. Fibrosis, for example, adds a
lot of extracellular-matrix protein, so every other protein makes up a smaller share. Median
normalization would then remove a real effect. MaxQuant's LFQ values are already normalized across all
75 runs, so the extra median step is a small correction. Treat it as a choice to check, not a
requirement (A8 and A9 show how much it changes the results).

```{r normalize, fig.height = 4.5}
log2fc <- function(M) rowMeans(M[, case_cols], na.rm = TRUE) - rowMeans(M[, ctrl_cols], na.rm = TRUE)

report <- function(M, label) {
  cat(sprintf("%-34s median log2FC (all proteins) %+.3f\n", label, median(log2fc(M))))
}

# Median normalization: subtract each sample's median, then add back the average median
med   <- apply(X, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE)
X_med <- sweep(X, 2, med) + mean(med)

report(X,     "as delivered (MaxLFQ-normalized)")
report(X_med, "median-normalized")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(6, 4, 3, 1))
for (v in list(list(X, "as delivered"), list(X_med, "median-normalized"))) {
  boxplot(v[[1]], names = short, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.6, outline = FALSE,
          col = grp_col, main = v[[2]], ylab = "log2 intensity")
}
legend("bottomright", fill = c("#1F77B4", "#D62728"), legend = c("control", "case"), cex = 0.8, bty = "n")
```

**Question 2.1** Do the sample medians already line up before normalization? (MaxQuant's LFQ algorithm
normalizes by itself.) Is the median log2 fold change near 0 in both versions?

**Question 2.2** Can you think of a reason why the assumption could still be violated in diseased heart
tissue? (Think of fibrosis: more extracellular matrix, relatively less of everything else.)

For the rest of Part A we use the median-normalized data when `params$normalize` is `true`. Set it to
`false` and re-knit to see what the choice costs.

```{r choose}
Xn <- if (isTRUE(params$normalize)) X_med else X
```

# A5 · Impute

A t-test needs numbers. Since most missing values are *low* proteins, a common choice (from Perseus) is
to fill them with random values from a narrow distribution near the detection limit: shifted down by
1.8 standard deviations and 0.3 times as wide.

```{r impute}
impute_perseus <- function(M, shift = 1.8, width = 0.3, seed = 0) {
  set.seed(seed)                                   # fixed seed, so the result is reproducible
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(M))) {                    # one sample at a time
    m <- mean(M[, j], na.rm = TRUE); s <- sd(M[, j], na.rm = TRUE)
    miss <- is.na(M[, j])
    M[miss, j] <- rnorm(sum(miss), m - shift * s, width * s)
  }
  M
}
Xi <- impute_perseus(Xn)

j <- 1
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
h_meas <- hist(Xn[, j], breaks = 60, plot = FALSE)
hist(Xn[, j], breaks = h_meas$breaks, col = adjustcolor("#1F77B4", 0.6), border = "white",
     xlab = "log2 intensity", main = paste("Imputed values sit at the low end (", short[j], ")"))
if (any(is.na(Xn[, j])))
  hist(Xi[is.na(Xn[, j]), j], breaks = 20, col = adjustcolor("#FF7F0E", 0.8), border = "white", add = TRUE)
legend("topright", fill = c(adjustcolor("#1F77B4", 0.6), "#FF7F0E"), legend = c("measured", "imputed"), bty = "n")
```

# A6 · Do the samples look right?

Before testing, check whether patients of the same group resemble each other more than the other
group. A PCA places each sample on the two axes along which the samples differ most.

```{r pca, fig.height = 5.5}
Z  <- Xi - rowMeans(Xi)                          # centre each protein on its own mean
sv <- svd(Z)                                     # singular value decomposition = PCA
pc <- sv$v[, 1:2] %*% diag(sv$d[1:2])            # sample coordinates on PC1 and PC2
explained <- sv$d^2 / sum(sv$d^2)                # share of the variation each PC explains

layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1, 1.15))
par(mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
plot(pc, pch = 19, cex = 1.4, col = grp_col,
     xlab = sprintf("PC1 (%.0f%%)", 100 * explained[1]),
     ylab = sprintf("PC2 (%.0f%%)", 100 * explained[2]), main = "PCA of the samples")
text(pc, labels = short, pos = 3, cex = 0.6)
legend("topright", col = c("#1F77B4", "#D62728"), pch = 19, legend = c("control", "case"), bty = "n")

C <- cor(Xi)
par(mar = c(6, 6, 3, 4))
image(1:ncol(C), 1:ncol(C), C, col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"), axes = FALSE,
      xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Sample correlation")
axis(1, at = 1:ncol(C), labels = short, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.5)
axis(2, at = 1:ncol(C), labels = short, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.5)
abline(h = length(ctrl_cols) + 0.5, v = length(ctrl_cols) + 0.5, col = "white", lwd = 2)
```

Unlike the benchmark (6 tightly controlled samples), these are different people. Expect the groups to
overlap: biological variation between patients is large, which is exactly why we need many replicates.

# A7 · Test every protein

A two-sample Welch t-test per protein (no equal-variance assumption), then the Benjamini–Hochberg
correction, because we run one test per protein.

```{r ttest}
welch_p <- function(M) {
  apply(M, 1, function(r) tryCatch(
    t.test(r[case_cols], r[ctrl_cols], var.equal = FALSE)$p.value,   # NAs are dropped by t.test
    error = function(e) NA_real_))
}

run_test <- function(M) {
  res <- data.frame(gene    = sub(";.*", "", ifelse(is.na(d$`Gene names`), "", d$`Gene names`)),
                    protein = d$`Majority protein IDs`,
                    log2FC  = log2fc(M),
                    p       = welch_p(M))
  res$q <- p.adjust(res$p, method = "BH")                    # Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values
  res$significant <- !is.na(res$q) & res$q < 0.05
  res
}

res <- run_test(Xi)
```

```{r volcano, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6}
dir_col <- ifelse(res$significant & res$log2FC > 0, "#D62728",
           ifelse(res$significant & res$log2FC < 0, "#1F77B4", "grey75"))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
plot(res$log2FC, -log10(res$p), pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = adjustcolor(dir_col, 0.6),
     xlab = sprintf("log2 fold change (%s / control)", params$case), ylab = "-log10 p",
     main = sprintf("Volcano plot — %s, %s", params$case, params$sex))
abline(v = 0, col = "grey40", lwd = 0.8)

# Label the strongest significant changes: far out on both axes
sig  <- res[res$significant & res$gene != "", ]
top  <- head(sig[order(-(-log10(sig$p) * abs(sig$log2FC))), ], 15)
text(top$log2FC, -log10(top$p), top$gene, pos = 3, cex = 0.6)
legend("topleft", pch = 19, col = c("#D62728", "#1F77B4", "grey75"), bty = "n",
       legend = c(sprintf("up (%d)", sum(dir_col == "#D62728")),
                  sprintf("down (%d)", sum(dir_col == "#1F77B4")), "not significant"))
```

# A8 · What did we find?

Here there is no ground truth, so we cannot count false positives. What we *can* do is look at how
many proteins we call, how much that depends on a fold-change cutoff, and how much it depends on the
analysis choices from A4 and A5.

```{r score}
score <- function(res, fc_cut = 0) {
  s <- res$significant & abs(res$log2FC) >= fc_cut
  data.frame(fold_change_cutoff = fc_cut, tested = sum(!is.na(res$p)),
             significant = sum(s), up = sum(s & res$log2FC > 0), down = sum(s & res$log2FC < 0))
}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 0.5, 1), function(c) score(res, c)))
```

The most significant proteins:

```{r top}
out <- res[order(res$q), ]
out$log2FC <- round(out$log2FC, 2)
head(out[, c("gene", "protein", "log2FC", "p", "q")], 25)
```

**How much do the choices matter?** The same test, run on four versions of the data:

```{r sensitivity}
choices <- list(
  "as delivered + imputed"      = impute_perseus(X),
  "median-norm. + imputed"      = impute_perseus(X_med),
  "as delivered, no imputation" = X,
  "median-norm., no imputation" = X_med
)
sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(choices), function(n) {
  r <- run_test(choices[[n]])
  cbind(analysis = n, score(r, 0), significant_at_FC_0.5 = score(r, 0.5)$significant)
}))
sens
```

**Question 2.3** How many proteins change at q < 0.05? How many survive a fold-change cutoff of
0.5 (≈1.4-fold) or 1 (2-fold)? Are the top hits biologically plausible for a heart under pressure
overload (aortic stenosis) or volume overload (mitral regurgitation)?

**Question 2.4** How much does the number of significant proteins change between the four versions in
the sensitivity table? Imputation adds many low, nearly identical values to one group when a protein is
missing mostly in the other: does imputation give you more or fewer hits, and do you trust those extra
hits?

```{r save}
outfile <- sprintf("PartA_results_%s_vs_%s_%s.csv", gsub("[^A-Za-z]+", "_", params$case),
                   gsub("[^A-Za-z]+", "_", sub(" \\(.*", "", params$control)), params$sex)
write.csv(out, outfile, row.names = FALSE)
cat("results written to", outfile, "\n")
```

# A9 · All comparisons

Now the same pipeline (A1 filter → A2 log → A3 two-thirds valid values per group → A4 median
normalization → A5 imputation → A7 Welch t-test + BH) for every pair of groups, separately for women
and men:

| Comparison | Question |
|---|---|
| aortic stenosis vs control | what changes under pressure overload? |
| mitral regurgitation vs control | what changes under volume overload? |
| aortic stenosis vs mitral regurgitation | what differs between the two diseases? |

The filtering is done separately for each comparison, so each one tests the proteins measured well in
*its* two groups.

```{r all-comparisons}
analyse <- function(case, control, sex, label, normalize = isTRUE(params$normalize)) {
  cc <- samples$column[samples$group == control & samples$sex == sex]
  ca <- samples$column[samples$group == case    & samples$sex == sex]
  dd <- pg[keep, ]                                              # A1: filtered protein table
  M  <- as.matrix(dd[, c(cc, ca)]); M[M == 0] <- NA; M <- log2(M)   # A2
  v  <- rowSums(!is.na(M[, cc])) >= ceiling(round(params$min_valid * length(cc), 6)) &
        rowSums(!is.na(M[, ca])) >= ceiling(round(params$min_valid * length(ca), 6))
  M  <- M[v, ]; dd <- dd[v, ]                                   # A3
  if (normalize) {                                              # A4
    med <- apply(M, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE)
    M   <- sweep(M, 2, med) + mean(med)
  }
  Mi <- impute_perseus(M)                                       # A5
  p  <- apply(Mi, 1, function(r) tryCatch(                      # A7
          t.test(r[ca], r[cc], var.equal = FALSE)$p.value, error = function(e) NA_real_))
  data.frame(comparison = label, sex = sex, n_case = length(ca), n_control = length(cc),
             gene    = sub(";.*", "", ifelse(is.na(dd$`Gene names`), "", dd$`Gene names`)),
             protein = dd$`Majority protein IDs`,
             log2FC  = rowMeans(Mi[, ca]) - rowMeans(Mi[, cc]),
             p = p, q = p.adjust(p, method = "BH"))
}

comparisons <- data.frame(
  case    = c("aortic stenosis", "mitral regurgitation", "aortic stenosis"),
  control = c(params$control,    params$control,         "mitral regurgitation"),
  label   = c("AS vs control",   "MR vs control",        "AS vs MR"))

all_res <- list()
for (sx in c("female", "male")) for (i in seq_len(nrow(comparisons))) {
  key <- paste(comparisons$label[i], sx, sep = " | ")
  all_res[[key]] <- analyse(comparisons$case[i], comparisons$control[i], sx, comparisons$label[i])
}

summary_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(all_res, function(r) {
  s <- !is.na(r$q) & r$q < 0.05
  data.frame(comparison = r$comparison[1], sex = r$sex[1],
             n_case = r$n_case[1], n_control = r$n_control[1], tested = nrow(r),
             significant = sum(s), up = sum(s & r$log2FC > 0), down = sum(s & r$log2FC < 0),
             significant_2fold = sum(s & abs(r$log2FC) >= 1))
}))
rownames(summary_tab) <- NULL
summary_tab
```

Up/down always means **higher/lower in the first group named** (e.g. "AS vs MR, up" = higher in
aortic stenosis than in mitral regurgitation).

```{r all-volcanoes, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 8}
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4, 3, 1))
for (key in names(all_res)) {
  r   <- all_res[[key]]
  sig <- !is.na(r$q) & r$q < 0.05
  col <- ifelse(sig & r$log2FC > 0, "#D62728", ifelse(sig & r$log2FC < 0, "#1F77B4", "grey75"))
  plot(r$log2FC, -log10(r$p), pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = adjustcolor(col, 0.6),
       xlab = "log2 fold change", ylab = "-log10 p",
       main = sprintf("%s (n = %d vs %d)", key, r$n_case[1], r$n_control[1]))
  abline(v = 0, col = "grey40", lwd = 0.8)
  top <- head(r[sig & r$gene != "", ][order(-(-log10(r$p[sig & r$gene != ""]) *
                                              abs(r$log2FC[sig & r$gene != ""]))), ], 8)
  text(top$log2FC, -log10(top$p), top$gene, pos = 3, cex = 0.55)
  legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, pch = 19, col = c("#D62728", "#1F77B4"),
         legend = c(sprintf("up (%d)", sum(col == "#D62728")), sprintf("down (%d)", sum(col == "#1F77B4"))))
}
```

**Do women and men agree?** For each comparison, how many proteins are significant in both sexes,
and do they change in the same direction?

```{r sex-overlap}
overlap <- do.call(rbind, lapply(comparisons$label, function(lab) {
  f <- all_res[[paste(lab, "female", sep = " | ")]]
  m <- all_res[[paste(lab, "male",   sep = " | ")]]
  b <- merge(f[, c("protein", "gene", "log2FC", "q")], m[, c("protein", "log2FC", "q")],
             by = "protein", suffixes = c("_F", "_M"))
  sf <- b$q_F < 0.05; sm <- b$q_M < 0.05
  data.frame(comparison = lab, tested_in_both = nrow(b),
             sig_female = sum(f$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), sig_male = sum(m$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
             sig_in_both = sum(sf & sm, na.rm = TRUE),
             same_direction = sum(sf & sm & sign(b$log2FC_F) == sign(b$log2FC_M), na.rm = TRUE),
             cor_log2FC = round(cor(b$log2FC_F, b$log2FC_M), 2))
}))
overlap
```

The most consistent changes (significant in both sexes, same direction) per comparison:

```{r consistent}
consistent <- do.call(rbind, lapply(comparisons$label, function(lab) {
  f <- all_res[[paste(lab, "female", sep = " | ")]]
  m <- all_res[[paste(lab, "male",   sep = " | ")]]
  b <- merge(f[, c("protein", "gene", "log2FC", "q")], m[, c("protein", "log2FC", "q")],
             by = "protein", suffixes = c("_F", "_M"))
  b <- b[b$q_F < 0.05 & b$q_M < 0.05 & sign(b$log2FC_F) == sign(b$log2FC_M), ]
  b <- b[order(-abs(b$log2FC_F + b$log2FC_M)), ]
  if (nrow(b) == 0) return(NULL)
  cbind(comparison = lab, head(b[, c("gene", "log2FC_F", "log2FC_M", "q_F", "q_M")], 10))
}))
consistent$log2FC_F <- round(consistent$log2FC_F, 2); consistent$log2FC_M <- round(consistent$log2FC_M, 2)
rownames(consistent) <- NULL
consistent
```

```{r save-all}
all_out <- do.call(rbind, all_res); rownames(all_out) <- NULL
write.csv(all_out, "PartA_results_all_comparisons.csv", row.names = FALSE)
cat("all results written to PartA_results_all_comparisons.csv\n")
```

**Question 2.5** Which comparison gives the most significant proteins? Look at the group sizes: there
are only 5 women with mitral regurgitation, and power depends on the smaller group. Are fewer hits
evidence that fewer proteins change?

**Question 2.6** How well do women and men agree (`cor_log2FC`, `same_direction`)? Are the
disagreements more likely to be real sex differences, or a lack of power in one sex?

**Question 2.7** Proteins that differ between aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation are candidates
for the different responses to pressure vs volume overload. Are they mostly proteins that also changed
against the controls, in only one of the two diseases?

**Question 2.8** Set `normalize: false` and re-knit. Which comparisons change the most? Do the
comparisons with the largest extracellular-matrix changes also show the largest median shift in A4?
